prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Prototype Controller Board BOM (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Part number" · longest unbreakable word 165px · one-line width 165px
  col 2: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 107px · one-line width 526px
  col 3: header "Qty" · longest unbreakable word 26px · one-line width 26px
  col 4: header "Unit price" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 70px
  col 5: header "Supplier" · longest unbreakable word 133px · one-line width 133px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"A bill of materials for identifying, sourcing and costing the parts needed for a prototype controller board.","reading":"Readers scan each row from part number and description to quantity, unit price and supplier, and compare quantities and prices down their columns. Long descriptions can set row height, leaving room for other cells to wrap without necessarily making the row taller.","groups":["Part number and description identify the component and its specifications.","Quantity and unit price are compact numerical fields used together for purchasing and cost comparison.","Supplier belongs with the purchasing fields and identifies where to source each part."],"keep_intact":["Part numbers and other component identifiers, so they can be copied and distinguished reliably.","Quantities and individual price values, so numbers and currency remain easy to compare.","Supplier names where possible, especially when they are used as search terms."],"may_wrap":["Descriptions at natural word and punctuation boundaries, while keeping individual specifications legible.","Headers at word boundaries where needed.","Supplier names at natural boundaries when the available width requires it."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r2A: widths [186, 165, 47, 91, 154] · table 644×686px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 106, 106, 83, 83, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 284px
Design r2B: widths [186, 128, 47, 91, 154] · table 607×872px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 153, 129, 106, 106, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 247px
Design r2C: widths [186, 145, 47, 91, 154] · table 624×849px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 129, 129, 106, 106, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 264px

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
